[Bacterial_Blight] Symptoms:
Bacterial Blight (Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. glycinea) typically begins with small, angular, reddish-brown lesions that are surrounded by a yellow halo. These lesions are most commonly found in the upper canopy because young leaves are the most susceptible to infection. As the disease progresses, the lesions can grow together to form large, irregularly shaped dead areas. Centers of older lesions often fall out, giving leaves a tattered appearance. The disease is favored by cool temperatures and can be more prevalent after rainstorms with high winds. Bacterial Blight is often confused with other diseases, but its specific symptom of leaf tattering distinguishes it from some similar diseases, like Septoria brown spot. | Often confused with: Bacterial_Pustule

[Septoria_brown_spot] Symptoms:
Septoria brown spot is the most common foliar disease of soybean, developing soon after planting and typically present throughout the growing season. Symptoms are typically mild during the vegetative stages and progress upward from lower leaves during grain fill. Infected young plants exhibit small, irregularly shaped, dark brown lesions on the unifoliate leaves. Lesions on later leaves are small and found on both leaf surfaces, often growing larger and forming irregularly shaped blotches. Infected leaves quickly turn yellow and drop. The disease starts in the lower canopy, and if conditions remain favorable, it will progress to the upper canopy, potentially leading to yield losses that depend on how far up the canopy the disease progresses during grain fill. The key difference between Septoria brown spot and Bacterial blight is that the latter shows tattering of leaf tissues, while Septoria does not. | Often confused with: Brown_Stem_Rot

[Bacterial_Pustule] Symptoms:
Bacterial Pustule (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines) symptoms typically appear mid to late season on the upper leaves of the plant. Initial lesions start as small, pale green specks with elevated centers, developing into larger, irregularly shaped infected areas. Each lesion is surrounded by a greenish-yellow halo. A pustule may form in the center of some lesions, usually visible on the lower leaf surface. Notably, bacterial pustule does not cause leaves to tatter as seen in bacterial blight. The disease thrives in hot, wet weather, and certain soybean varieties may be particularly susceptible, while others are marketed as resistant. In comparison to Bacterial Blight, which causes tattered leaves and has angular, reddish-brown lesions with yellow halos, bacterial pustule is characterized by its distinct pale green specks and the absence of leaf tattering. | Often confused with: Bacterial_Blight
